evidence: The plan refuses the seed's frame outright: it splits the seed into H1 (customers sign LTAs — 'close to a truism') and H2 (durability), states 'the prior from the 2021-2023 semiconductor cycle points the other way,' names Microchip/ON/Wolfspeed vs the TI abstainer, and pre-commits to the bear null: 'shortage guidance plus a rush of LTAs is a cycle-peak marker, not a durability signal.' It also carries the specific bear mechanisms — 'The cycle-peak problem is the central threat,' 'Double ordering... Measure backlog-to-shipment *conversion*, never backlog level,' 'Enforceability is social, not legal... Expect renegotiation, and code for it,' the take-or-pay/cash-collateral cut ('whether the resulting agreements carry customer cash — prepayment or deposit — versus non-binding capacity reservations'), and 'Price versus volume.' The critique ratifies and operationalizes that reframe rather than restating it: 'The honest null ("shortage + LTA wave is a late-cycle sell signal") is the right null and I believe it.' It then pushes the frame further with its own version of the gold flaw — 'The treatment is a disclosure decision, not a shortage... The treated set is not "firms with shortages," it is "firms that chose to publicise shortages," and that choice is made by the same commercial strategy that produces the LTA book. Every H1 coefficient is then partly definitional.' Its recommended 'cheaper version' is exactly the gold test: trace 'announced contract face value at signing -> subsequent RPO and contract-liability disclosure -> revenue actually recognised through 2024-25 -> any renegotiation, de-commit, deferral or quiet disappearance in the 10-K language. Compute a realisation ratio per firm,' against 'a deliberate abstainer control group (TI is the obvious one).' It does not, however, independently surface the competitor-capacity-entry leg of the bear case.
missed: Competitor and greenfield capacity response — the shortage itself pulls in new supply (rival expansions, CHIPS/China mature-node fabs) that lands precisely as the LTAs mature. The plan only moderates on the focal firm's own capex ramp; the critique never notes that industry-level capacity additions, not firm capex, are the mechanism that guts the LTA book, and no industry capacity/utilisation series is in the data section.

The critique flags ORDBKLG as annual-only and unusable in a quarterly window, but never connects that to the plan's principal double-ordering defense — 'measure backlog-to-shipment conversion, never backlog level' has no quarterly data source, so the phantom-demand check silently cannot be run. The obvious substitute, customers' own inventory days (a customer-side panel), is proposed by neither document.

The 'cheaper version' reproduces the selection bug the critique just diagnosed: picking '20-25 firms with large disclosed LTA/capacity-commitment books' selects on the disclosure decision exactly as the panel does, and the abstainer arm is effectively n=1 (TI), whose downcycle path is driven by its own inventory-build strategy and analog mix rather than by LTA abstention. No confound discussion.

The realisation ratio is treated as a clean statistic. Announced face value is multi-year, often non-binding, frequently amended without an 8-K, and denominators are not comparable across firms; a ratio near 1.0 can be produced by silently re-signing at lower volume or lower price. The measure needs a volume-and-price decomposition or it will flatter committers.

Neither document defines durability against the right counterfactual: an LTA may simply re-paper demand the customer would have placed anyway, shifting recognition timing rather than creating persistence. Without that, a positive H2 can be a relabeling artifact.

Take-or-pay is coded as a binary (binding / prepaid / termination fee) with no attention to the price term. An LTA struck at peak ASPs is the thing most likely to be renegotiated; a volume commitment at a floating or MFN price is a materially different instrument. The critique reviews the tag coverage but not the economics of what is being counted.
manufactured: Kill-shot #1 misreads the plan's pre-registered primary. The critique asserts 'Primary durability outcome: us-gaap:RevenueRemainingPerformanceObligation' and concludes 'The study as designed is a 2018-2023 study.' The plan pre-registers 'the t+8 revenue-path coefficient' as the H2 primary (line 84) — an outcome available from 2003. The ASC 606 coverage hole is real and worth raising, but it demotes one supporting outcome; it does not collapse the sample window, and the drawdown, AR(1), volatility and gross-margin durability measures the critique itself later recommends are already in the plan's Durability block.

'The plan's stop rule fires on day one, not in week three' conflates two different things. The stop rule is conditioned on event counts outside 2020-2022, not on outcome-variable availability. Outcome coverage and event supply are separate constraints; presenting the accounting-standard date as triggering an event-count kill overstates a valid point into a false one.

Similarly overstated: 'two of the three primary outcome variables... do not exist before 2018.' The plan names three triangulated H1 measures, of which only the XBRL contract-liability tag is post-2018; the 8-K/EX-10 count and the normalized transcript-mention measure run the full span. The critique's own remedy ('pick outcomes that exist across the full span') is partly already in the plan it is faulting.

'The market-outcome block... is attached to no hypothesis' is thin — the plan states its purpose ('to answer whether any of this is already priced'), which for an investability-oriented study is a hypothesis. Recommending it be cut on that basis is a stylistic preference dressed as a design break.
verdict_line: Plan refuses the seed's frame outright and pre-commits to the bear null, so there was no gold flaw left to catch — the critique correctly ratifies that and adds a sharper version of it (treatment is a disclosure choice, not a shortage) plus the right two-week realisation-ratio substitute, but it oversells its headline kill by mistaking RPO for the pre-registered H2 primary and never asks who else is building capacity while these LTAs run.
